newsitem.title: UK: UK voters say enough is enough - Reuters/NOP poll.
newsitem.headline: UK voters say enough is enough - Reuters/NOP poll.

text.p: Britain's voters could send the ruling Conservative party packing after 18 years of government simply because they feel "it's time for a change", an exclusive Reuters/NOP poll showed on Tuesday.

Given a choice of 10 categories for the most important factor to influence which way they would vote, 26 percent -- the equal highest number -- of those surveyed in the poll opted for desire for change.
Another 26 percent said that liking the policies of the party they intended to vote for was the main factor.
The poll of 1,065 people in 52 constituencies was conducted on March 14.
In what promises to be a long, dirty campaign, voters said they would ignore the appeal of a party leader or candidate and brush aside past voting habits when they elect a new government on May 1.
Only seven percent said the choice of party leader would have any effect on the way they would vote.
Only 15 percent said they would support a party for traditional reasons, while liking or disliking the local candidate was virtually irrelevant.
Respondents were asked: "Choose the main issue which will influence your vote."
Issue percentage
It's time for a change 26
I like the policies of the party 26
Tradition/I always vote for this party 15
I dislike the policies of the other parties 11
I like the leader of the party 4
I dislike the leader of the other party/s 3
Don't know 3
I like the candidate 2
I will be using my vote tactically 2
I dislike the candidate of the other party/s 1
Others 8
Thirty-six percent of respondents said education policies would influence their vote, although there is no longer a clear gap between the two major parties on the issue.
Falling educational standards have prompted promises of action by all parties.
Labour leader Tony Blair has turned his back on traditional Labour policies in an effort to win middle class votes.

He has promised not to kill off schools that select pupils via competition for places and says schools should have more control over their own affairs, an idea championed by Prime Minister John Major.
The Liberal Democrats have promised to invest two billion sterling ($3.2 billion) in education by adding one penny to the standard rate of income tax.
The National Health Service (NHS) was also a crucial issue, with 32 percent of respondents saying health policies would influence their vote.

Overall results put opposition Labour further into the lead with 54 percent of the vote against 29 percent for the Conservative party. Support for the Liberal Democrats slumped to 11 percent with minor parties taking a further six percent.
